To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the local environment of the fluorine atom can be described by a fluorine fingerprint and that the LEF fragment library, combined with NMR ligand based screening, represents an efficient and effective tool for the identification of fragments relevant for the binding of the target protein.
a novel strategy for the selection and design of fluorinated chemical libraries is presented, based on the local environment of the fluorine atom.
a novel fluorine-based fingerprint descriptor, named LEF, was used to design a fluorine fragment library and to perform (19)F ligand-based screening.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a novel approach to the fragment-based drug discovery that combines a fragment library design strategy based on the local environment of the fluorine atom and a NMR-based screening approach that allows the detection of multiple hits present within the same mixture and the identification of ligands with weak affinity for the receptor.
the development of a new approach that can be easily implemented in the drug discovery process and that is able to provide a fast and reliable identification of fragments that bind a given target.
the design and synthesis of a library of fluorinated fragments, the LEF library.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the LEF library and the NMR screening approach described here represent a powerful tool in the fragment-based discovery of novel ligands.

the LEF library is a valuable tool in a fragment-based screening approach for the identification of weak affinity binders, and that the use of (19)F ligand-based screening in combination with the LEF library allows the detection of multiple hits within a tested mixture.
the described LEF library, combined with NMR-based ligand screening, represents a very useful and powerful approach for fragment-based drug discovery projects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the LEF library is able to provide information that cannot be obtained with other libraries, thus representing a complementary approach for fragment-based drug discovery projects.
LEF, a fluorine-containing library, can be used as a screening tool to identify fragments with a high affinity for a protein of interest.
the LEF library is a useful tool in the fragment-based screening process.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the fluorophilic environment of proteins is a powerful tool for the design of fluorinated fragment libraries, and that the use of NMR screening in combination with the fluorophilic character of proteins is an efficient approach to identify the initial fragments for the fragment-based drug design process.

the LEF library, in combination with NMR ligand based screening experiments represents an effective and sensitive tool for initial fragment identification within the fragment-based drug discovery process.

fluorophilicity of a receptor can be exploited to detect very weak-affinity binders and multiple hits in a single NMR experiment, thus increasing the chances of identifying a starting fragment in a fragment-based drug design project.
